sections.heading: How to summarize text
sections.body:
Start with the text you want shorter. It can be an article, a report, an essay or a set of notes. Paste it into the box, or upload a file up to 15 MB. The summarizer reads what you give it and writes a summary in the length you pick.

1. Open the [summarizer](https://summarizer.lazur.app/).
2. Paste your text into the box, or upload a file up to 15 MB.
3. Pick Short, Medium or Bullet points.
4. Run the summary, then read it next to the original.
5. Copy the result with one click.

**The summary keeps the important facts, names and numbers.** It cuts the parts you do not need, so a long report becomes something you can read in a few minutes.

sections.heading: Choose the length you need
sections.body:
You pick one of three lengths before you run the summary. Pick the one that matches what you will do with the result.

- **Short** gives the shortest summary. Use it when you only need the gist of an article before you decide whether to read the rest.
- **Medium** gives a fuller summary with more of the context. Use it for a report or a chapter that you still want to understand in some detail.
- **Bullet points** gives the main ideas as a list. Use it to scan a meeting note, a study guide or a long email thread.

If the first summary is too thin, run it again with Medium. If it is still more than you need, switch to Short.

sections.heading: Check the summary before you use it
sections.body:
A summary is a shortened version of your text, so it can miss a point. Before you share or quote it, check the details against the original. Look for every name, date, price and number in the summary, and find each one in your source.

Watch for conditions. Words such as unless, only if and except often disappear in a short summary, and they can change the meaning of a sentence. If a fact in the summary is not in your text, do not use it.

Summaries work best on text that is clear to begin with. If your source is full of unclear shorthand, the summary can be hard to follow. Fix the obvious typos first, or add a line at the top that says what the text is about, then run it again.

sections.heading: Free use and file size
sections.body:
The summarizer is free. You get 3 runs a day. After you leave an email, you get 3 more. You do not need an account to use the free runs, and you can copy the result with one click.

You can upload a file up to 15 MB. If your file is bigger, split it into sections, summarize each section, then read the summaries together. The summary usually comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds, so you can try a short paragraph and then a full article without waiting long.

sections.heading: What happens to your text
sections.body:
Your text is sent to Lazur's servers and processed by Google Gemini to write the summary. So the text you paste or upload leaves your computer.

Treat the summarizer like any online service. Do not paste passwords, bank or card details, ID numbers or private medical records. If the text is confidential, check your organization's rules before you send it.

sections.heading: How to summarize your notes
sections.body:
Notes are often short phrases, half sentences and lists. A summary of them works best when the notes are readable. Paste them as they are, or upload a file with your notes, then choose a length.

4. Run the summary and read it against your notes.

Read the summary once on its own, then once next to your notes. The first read shows you the main points. The second read shows you what the summary left out.

sections.heading: Pick the length for your notes
sections.body:
- **Bullet points** turns the notes into a list of main ideas. Use it when you want to review before a test or a meeting.
- **Medium** keeps more of the context, so the link between ideas stays clear. Use it when your notes cover one long topic.
- **Short** gives the quickest overview. Use it to decide which parts of your notes to reread first.

If you are not sure, run the summary twice with two lengths and keep the one that helps you remember more.

sections.heading: When the notes are hard to read
sections.body:
Messy notes make a messy summary. Before you run it, fix the obvious gaps. Expand short forms you will not remember later, such as 'pol econ' or 'Q3 rev'. Add one line at the top that says what the notes are about, such as 'Biology lecture on cell division'. Then run the summary again.

If the summary drops a point you wrote down, check your notes for that point. The summary is a shortened version, so a detail you think is important can be left out. Add it back by hand.

sections.heading: What happens to your notes

Your notes are sent to Lazur's servers and processed by Google Gemini to write the summary. So the text leaves your computer when you run it.

Do not paste private or confidential notes, such as health details, passwords, bank information or personal information about other people, unless you are comfortable sending that text to a service.

sections.heading: What the size limit is

sections.heading: Choose the length for a long document

sections.heading: Check the summary against the source

sections.heading: Summarize text in your Mac browser
sections.body:
You do not need to install anything on your Mac. Open the summarizer in the browser you use, paste your text, and run it.

sections.heading: Use Summarize in macOS Writing Tools
sections.body:
macOS has a built-in option called Writing Tools. It can summarize text you have selected while you write. Apple's steps are below.

1. While you are writing, select the text you want to summarize.
2. Control-click the selected text, choose Writing Tools, then choose Show Writing Tools.
3. Click Summarize to condense the text, or click Key Points to pull out only the most important points.
4. When you are finished, click Done.

Apple's full guide is at [Writing Tools on Mac](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/writing-tools-write-improve-summarize-mchldcd6c260/mac). Apple says Apple Intelligence features are not available in all languages or regions, and usage limits may apply, so check the guide for your Mac and language.

sections.heading: Which one to use
sections.body:
Use Writing Tools when you are already writing in an app that supports it and you want a summary of a selection. Use this summarizer when you have a file to upload, when you want to choose Short, Medium or Bullet points, or when you want the summary in your browser.

The browser version accepts files up to 15 MB, so it suits a long document saved as one file. For a short passage you are writing right now, the selection tool is usually quicker.

sections.heading: Check the summary on your Mac
sections.body:
Either tool can leave out a fact or change a detail. Read the summary next to the original text. Check each name, number and date. Before you send a summary to someone else, make sure it says what the source says.

Mac users often switch between a browser and a document. Keep the original open in one window and the summary in another, so you can compare them quickly without losing your place.

sections.heading: Free use and privacy

The summarizer is free, with 3 runs a day and 3 more after you leave an email. You do not need an account for the free runs.

Your text is sent to Lazur's servers and processed by Google Gemini to write the summary. Do not paste passwords, bank or card details, or private health information. Writing Tools is a separate Apple feature, so read Apple's guide to see how it handles your text.

If you write on your Mac every day, Lazur types for you in any app. Hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in.

faq.q: How do I summarize on a Mac?
faq.a: Open the summarizer in your Mac browser, paste your text or upload a file up to 15 MB, pick a length, and run it. Or select text in an app, Control-click it, choose Writing Tools, then Show Writing Tools, and click Summarize.

faq.q: Can I summarize text on a Mac for free?
faq.a: Yes. The browser summarizer is free: 3 runs a day, and 3 more after you leave an email. Writing Tools is a separate built-in macOS option, and whether it is available depends on your Mac and your language.

faq.q: Does the Mac summarizer need an app?
